idiom_name: scala.util.Either[+A, +B] with Left as the reason and Right as the value
implementation_notes: scala.util.Either is in the standard library: Left is the failure and Right the success by convention, the type is right-biased (since 2.12 map and flatMap operate on the Right side and return a Left unchanged), and because Either defines both it composes inside a for comprehension, where the first Left short-circuits the remaining steps. Pattern matching over the two cases is exhaustive, and toOption/fold/getOrElse cover the conversions, so the classic structure does not need to be rebuilt - only the convention (Left carries the reason) has to be kept.
pitfalls: for comprehensions over Either cannot use guards or refutable patterns - withFilter and the pattern-matching machinery are not defined, so `for { i <- either; if i > 0 } yield i` fails to compile; convert with toOption first.

Because Left is not the projected side, missing type arguments in a for can leave the right type inferred as Nothing, and the following expression then fails to type or resolves an ambiguous overload (the scaladoc's own example).
Either short-circuits on the first Left: if the caller needs every validation error at once, that is an accumulating validation type, not Either.
A thrown exception inside a mapped function still escapes the Either, so a handled failure becomes a crash; catch at the boundary (Try/try-catch) and convert to Left there.
